definition: Quick sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that selects a 'pivot' element from the array and partitions the other elements into two sub-arrays, according to whether they are less than or greater than the pivot.
details: Quick sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that selects a 'pivot' element from the array and partitions the other elements into two sub-arrays, according to whether they are less than or greater than the pivot. The sub-arrays are then sorted recursively.

explainer.lead: Quick sort is a widely used sorting algorithm that is fast on large, randomized data. Its divide-and-conquer design makes it a common default for general-purpose sorting.

tiers.eli5: It’s like sorting a deck of cards by picking one card and putting all lower cards to its left and higher cards to its right, then repeating on each pile.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it for in-place sorting with good average performance; a pitfall is poor pivot choice causing worst-case quadratic time, and it is not stable.
tiers.paperLevel: A divide-and-conquer comparison sort that selects a pivot, partitions other elements into sub-arrays of less-than and greater-than the pivot, and sorts those recursively; it works in-place, is not stable, and has average O(n log n) but worst-case O(n²) time.

explainer.example: Sorting [3, 6, 1, 8] with pivot 3 partitions into [1] and [6, 8], then recursively sorts to [1, 3, 6, 8].
